body: Just out of curiosity, is there a useful use case for this? I wonder why authors would add such links to their page other than for somewhat comedic purposes maybe. I mean the author would have no control over which website he links to and very limited control over which content he links to.

The author already has no control since they have no idea what the search engine will surface. Search engines change, results change, some are customized per user. Often I put links to searches in descriptions. The latest today was an article on graphics programming and I wanted to say something like, > `If this works you should see no Moiré patterns`. For the link I would often put [`https://google.com/search?q=Moiré pattern`](https://google.com/search?q=Moiré%20pattern) but it occured to me it would be better to use a url that opens the user's preferred search engine. Any argument against seems like an argument that would apply for default search engines period? In the same way hovering over a link shows where it's going to go, it would show a "search:" indicating it's going to go to the user's preferred search engine. Further, people chose search engines for a variety of reasons. They may find one has better answers. More localized answers. More privacy. Etc.... They may not want to go to alternative search engines. I can even imagine more enhanced results because by making the link "search:" the browser knows the content of the link is a search so it can use the user's choice to surface hover results. It could even go further, inferring from the content of the page the link is on the context of the search. `search:windows` on homedepot.com is probably about windows made of glass whereas `search:windows` on stackoverflow.com is probably about Microsoft windows.

> Often I put links to searches in descriptions. The latest today was an article on graphics programming and I wanted to say something like, > > > `If this works you should see no Moiré patterns`. > > For the link I would often put [`https://google.com/search?q=Moiré pattern`](https://google.com/search?q=Moir%C3%A9%20pattern) Well, you are free as an author to do that. But as a reader I do not find that useful. To the contrary, I would find it distracting. If you make "Moiré pattern" a link, I would expect that you did that to point to information about Moiré patterns that you, as an author, have identified as complementing your article in a useful way. But my expectation would not be fulfilled, if I clicked on the link in your example and were send to a search engine. I know where to find and how to use a search engine myself when I need one. (And if I didn't know what a Moiré pattern is and wanted to look that up, I wouldn't even choose a search engine, personally, but go directly to an encyclopedia). So my perception would be that your link disctracts readers and leads them away from your content for no good reason. I would recommend not to do that. > In the same way hovering over a link shows where it's going to go, it would show a "search:" indicating it's going to go to the user's preferred search engine. Further, people chose search engines for a variety of reasons. They may find one has better answers. More localized answers. More privacy. Etc.... They may not want to go to alternative search engines. I can select any word or group of words on a webpage in my browser (Firefox right now, but it works similarly in other browsers), right-click to get the browser's context menu and opt to search for the selected text using my preferred search engine. That's three clicks and it works for every piece of text that I want. I do not need webpage authors to predetermine for me what I can search for. > I can even imagine more enhanced results because by making the link "search:" the browser knows the content of the link is a search so it can use the user's choice to surface hover results. It could even go further, inferring from the content of the page the link is on the context of the search. `search:windows` on homedepot.com is probably about windows made of glass whereas `search:windows` on stackoverflow.com is probably about Microsoft windows. I don't see how that would be useful for me as a user in this example either. I go to stackoverflow.com to find user-generated answers to specific problems. I'd also be happy to get an answer with a link there that leads me directly to e.g. a microsoft.com page that contains the solution to my problem. But I would not be satisfied to be served a link that leads me just away from stackoverflow.com and e.g. to a Google search for "[Microsoft] windows". If I wanted my preferred search engine instead of stackoverflow, I would have gone there in the first place.

We'll just have to agree to disagree

As the author of the link, I don't want to have to go find an article on Moiré patterns. One that might disappear or one that might not be the best. That's the whole point of the search, the search is up to date and, if the search engine is good, should surface the current best article.

Further, I don't want to take responsibility for some link that might be good today but got abandoned and turned into SEO bait or an ad for malware. Nor do I want to link to a specific search engine and therefore implicitly endorse it.

As for why put it in a link, that's to highlight to go read something on the topic rather than have to spell out .... "Moiré patterns, if you don't know what these are you should go manually search now an read an article on them before you continue". You might be smart enough to do that but my readers are often not. They have to be slightly lead. The balance for me is to leave a link to a search.

Note: I often leave links to searches in stack overflow questions for more details. Specifically because the search engine provides multiple resources so rather than leaving 20 links I leave a link that leads to 20 links. Hopefully one of them helps the user in the way they need help rather than me picking a single one that doesn't resonate with them.
